name: Ioane of Zedazeni
notable: Leader of the mission from Mesopotamia. Chose Mount Zedazeni north of Mtskheta. Lived in ascetic solitude with bears as companions.
martyrdom: Died peacefully around 573 AD. Buried inside Zedazeni Church.

name: Stephane of Khirsa
notable: Sent east into fertile Kakheti. Built a major cathedral dedicated to Archdeacon Stephen near the Khirsa river.
martyrdom: Passed away peacefully; his tomb is preserved near the altar in Khirsa Cathedral.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: While most of his fellow Syrian monks looked for quiet caves or remote forest ridges to pray in solitude, Abibos took on a much more public, high-stakes role. Becoming the Bishop of Nekresi in Kakheti, he stepped directly into a cultural battleground where Sasanian Persian influence was strong and Zoroastrian fire temples stood right alongside Christian communities. Instead of retreating from the world, he actively traveled across the eastern mountains, converting locals and openly challenging Persian religious authority.

The story everyone remembers about Abibos—and the reason Nekresi still has a quirky culinary rule today—comes down to a single bucket of water. Exhausted by watching local Georgians bow to a sacred Zoroastrian flame, Abibos walked straight into the fire temple and poured water over the brazier, extinguishing the "eternal" fire on the spot. Legend also connects Nekresi with a clever survival trick during a later Muslim raid: locals reportedly slaughtered pigs and poured pork blood around the monastery gates, causing the attackers to turn back in disgust. To this day, Nekresi is the only church complex in Georgia where pork is traditionally allowed at the festive table.

Extinguishing the royal Persian fire was treated as treason. Persian soldiers arrested Abibos, beat him, and marched him toward the governor of Marzpan in Mtskheta. Near the village of Rekha, he was stoned to death and his body dragged outside the walls to be eaten by wild beasts—though local chronicles note the animals refused to touch him. Monks initially buried him at Samtavro before his relics were eventually brought back beneath the episcopal church in Mtskheta (Samtavro Monastery). Today, he is venerated by the Georgian Orthodox Church as a Hieromartyr (Saint and Martyr) and the spiritual protector of Kakheti.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Architecturally, Nekresi isn't a single building, but a compact medieval town perched high on a steep wooded ridge overlooking the Alazani Valley. Its oldest surviving gem—the tiny fourth-century basilica built even before Abibos arrived—is one of the earliest Christian stone churches in Georgia, so small you almost have to duck inside. Around it, the complex expanded across centuries: you'll see a 6th–7th century three-church basilica (a uniquely Georgian layout where three naves are separated by solid walls), a 9th-century domed church, the ruins of a two-story bishop's palace, a defensive tower, and an ancient marani (wine cellar) with massive clay qvevri buried in the stone floor.

Today, Nekresi operates as an active men's monastery and one of Kakheti's most atmospheric historic sites. Because the road up the mountain is dangerously steep, visitors leave their cars at the bottom and take a shuttle bus up through the dense forest—emerging onto breezy stone terraces where monks still live and the entire Alazani plain stretches out below like a map.

name: Tate of Shuamta
notable: Settled in the dense deciduous woods of Tsiv-Gombori mountains, building the early Christian basilica of Shuamta.
martyrdom: Died in tranquility surrounded by disciples; revered as a protector of mountaineers and travelers.

name: Zenon of Ikhalto
notable: Founded the Holy Transfiguration cloister, laying foundations for Georgia's famous Academy of philosophy and science.
martyrdom: Reposed in peace of old age; enshrined within the Church of the Holy Spirit at Ikhalto.

name: Davit of Gareja
notable: Initially dwelt on Mount Mtatsminda in Tbilisi, then retreated south into the harsh semi-desert caves of Gareja.
martyrdom: Reposed in peace in extreme old age. Refused to enter Jerusalem out of humility.

name: Ioseb of Alaverdi
notable: Settled in the wild plains of Alaverdi. His hermitage later grew into the monumental 11th-century Alaverdi Cathedral.
martyrdom: Fell asleep in the Lord peacefully in 570 AD. His tomb became an ancient center of pilgrimage.

name: Anton of Martqopi
notable: Brought an authentic Image of Christ on a clay tile (Mandylion) to Georgia. Lived atop a tall stone tower as a stylite.
martyrdom: Spent his final 15 years atop his pillar in prayer, reposing peacefully around 590 AD.

name: Ise of Tsilkani
notable: Established solitary prayer cells and churches in the valleys near Tsilkani and Mtskheta.
martyrdom: Lived to extreme old age and passed into eternal rest in peace at his retreat in Tsilkani.

name: Shio of Mgvime
notable: Lived in a remote limestone canyon near Mtskheta. Thousands gathered to form Georgia's largest monastery.
martyrdom: Voluntarily spent the last 15 years sealed deep in an underground pit tomb in ceaseless prayer.

name: Isidore of Samtavisi
notable: Established a monastic community on the banks of the Lekhura river. Renowned for boundless charity and discipline.
martyrdom: Died peacefully; buried inside Samtavisi Cathedral, famed for its masterwork stone carvings.

name: Piros of Breti
notable: Founded a monastic cloister at Breti. Renowned for unceasing empathy toward leprosy patients and the poor.
martyrdom: Died peacefully; buried inside the Mother of God Church at Breti Monastery.

name: Mikhail of Ulumbo
notable: Established a flourishing spiritual center at Mount Ulumbo, overturning remaining pagan practices.
martyrdom: Reposed in peace after establishing an influential monastic cloister in central Georgia.
